issue_context.title: BUG: `pd.testing.assert_frame_equal` does not propagate precision to interval dtype
issue_context.body:
### 

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
df1 = pd.DataFrame()
df1[0] = pd.arrays.IntervalArray.from_tuples([(1.0, 2.0)])

df2 = pd.DataFrame()
df2[0] = pd.arrays.IntervalArray.from_tuples([(1.0000000000001, 2.0)])

# Using very large tolerances do not propagate to the interval dtype, since this assert fails:
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df1, df2, check_exact=False, rtol=10., atol=10.)
```


### Issue Description

It seems that `pd.testing.assert_frame_equal` does not propagate chosen tolerances for `interval` dtype comparison.

### Expected Behavior

df1 = pd.DataFrame()
df1[0] = pd.arrays.IntervalArray.from_tuples([(1.0, 2.0)])
df2 = pd.DataFrame()
df2[0] = pd.arrays.IntervalArray.from_tuples([(1.0000000000001, 2.0)])
# This test should pass...
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df1, df2, check_exact=False, rtol=10., atol=10.)

comments: Thanks for reporting this @stephanegaiffas! Confirmed on master, looks like `assert_interval_array_equal` doesn't support tolerance arguments so they just end up ignored. Looks to also be an issue for some other ExtensionDtypes like `sparse`.

The function calls assert_interval_array_equal() within assert_series_equal() after assert_frame_equal(). Can I create another function, assert_interval_array_almost_equal(), that would take in the relative and absolute tolerances because assert_interval_array_equal() checks if the values are exactly equal and doesn't pass down the keyword arguments?

review_comments: Please add gh reference
Done
Remove comment
Done
Can't these tolerance arguments just be added to `assert_interval_array_equal`? Why is a separate function necessary?

`assert_interval_array_equal` calls `assert_equal` which checks that the numbers being compared are exactly equal. Hence the decision to use assert_interval_array_almost_equal that takes tolerance and calls assert_almost_equal

`assert_equal` takes `**kwargs` which are passed into the other `assert_*` functions that appear to accept `rtol` and `atol` so I imagine it should be possible to integrate this directly into `assert_interval_array_equal`
Could `assert_interval_array_equal` dispatch to `assert_almost_equal` if tolerances are specified?
Yea similar to this.

👍🏾
How do I address situations where only one of `rtol` or `atol` is passed in?
You can just pass through the kwargs like `assert_almost_equal(left._left, right._left, **kwargs)`

Got it.
Thanks.

It looks like I may have to set a default `rtol` and `atol`.
`assert_frame_equal` takes in tolerance and calls `assert_series_equal` which also takes in tolerance, but tolerance isn't passed in when `assert_interval_array_equal` is called and I can't pass in `**kwargs` because it's not defined. 
If I pass in `rtol=rtol, atol=atol`, then the branching logic we want to implement in `assert_intterval_array_equal` will always evaluate to be true.
What should I do in this case?
Yeah `rtol` and `atol` may need to be added explicitly in `assert_interval_array_equal` and other places
So I should stick to using `assert_equal` and pass tolerance in to the end of the various function calls? Should I abandon using `assert_allmost_equal`?
`assert_equal` would be ideal to minimize the code diff. In the end, we want to avoid creating a whole new function for testing intervals with tolerances.
Thanks for all your comments @mroeschke ! I've made the edits in a new pull request [here](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/48295)
Please just update this pull request instead of opening up a new pull request.
Apologies 😬. I'll update this PR shortly

On the previous new pull request I opened that got closed, Jeff mentioned that `array_equivalent` is meant for testing equality and not closeness, therefore I can't pass tolerance into it. What alternative approach should I take?
No worries. The alternative is to use `assert_almost_equal` in place of `assert_equal` if possible.
Got it! Thanks.
